"""Layer 15 MLP down_proj component 448: a weak, context-driven readout.

What it is: a single rank-one piece of the MLP output projection. Its activation is
the MLP hidden state dotted with one fixed direction, scaled. That direction is
mostly hidden unit 448 (about a fifth of its variance) plus a diffuse readout of
about a thousand other units. Nothing in the token text explains it: the token
identity, the previous token, and simple character classes each explain about 1%
of its variance or less. It is essentially zero-mean noise with std about 0.29.

What this program does: it predicts only the one trend that is visible. Counting
positions from the start of each document, the activation is about zero at the
first token, slightly negative for the next few tokens, and slightly positive
once the document is well under way. The program predicts those three levels and
nothing else. It explains roughly 0.1% of the variance.
"""

READS = ()


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    doc = prefix.document_ids[-1]
    if carry is None or carry[1] != doc:
        pos = 0  # first token of a document (or of the packed row)
    else:
        pos = carry[0] + 1
    if pos == 0:
        value = 0.0
    elif pos < 16:
        value = -0.02
    elif pos < 64:
        value = 0.0
    else:
        value = 0.02
    return (pos, doc), value

"""Layer 15 MLP hidden unit 449: the component down_proj:449 is this one SwiGLU unit.

What it does, as far as a short program can say: it is near zero in ordinary prose and
drifts positive inside source code, most strongly on loop and index names (i, j, k, idx,
item, key, id, ...) written in code. The spikes are not predictable from token identity
or from any simple context feature; the best compact rule found explains under 1% of
its variance.

Prediction, from the last 32 tokens of the same document:
  density = share of those tokens that look like code (contain a bracket, operator,
            semicolon or a code keyword)
  value   = 0.67 * density + 2.2 * density * [current token is an index/item name]
            + 0.15 * [current token is an index/item name]
"""

from collections.abc import Mapping
import re

READS: tuple[str, ...] = ()

CODE = re.compile(r"[{}()\[\];=<>+\-*/&|!%.:]|\b(for|while|if|return|def|var|int|new)\b")
INDEX_NAMES = {"i", "j", "k", "n", "idx", "item", "key", "id", "_id", "Id", "Item",
               "entry", "elem", "token", "index", "digit", "vertex", "line"}
WINDOW = 32


def step(carry, prefix, upstream: Mapping):
    docs = prefix.document_ids
    last = len(docs) - 1
    lo = last
    while lo > 0 and docs[lo - 1] == docs[last] and last - lo < WINDOW - 1:
        lo -= 1
    recent = prefix.token_strings[lo:]
    density = sum(bool(CODE.search(s)) for s in recent) / len(recent)
    is_index = prefix.token_strings[-1].strip() in INDEX_NAMES
    value = 0.67 * density + (2.2 * density + 0.15 if is_index else 0.0)
    return carry, float(value)

"""A word-level reading of layers.15.mlp.down_proj component 450.

What the component does: its output direction promotes words like "associate",
"association" and "associated" in the next-token distribution. Its activation is
high on words that state a link or connection between things (correlate, coincide,
relationship, linked, tied, in conjunction with, equivalent) and, more weakly, on the
linking preposition that follows one of them (with, between, to) within a few tokens.

This program puts a positive value on those words and their linking prepositions, and
the component's typical value (about -0.02) everywhere else. It is a rough description:
word rules explain only a tiny share of the activation's variance. The largest negative
values sit on statistics, data-analysis and technical wording, which no word list here
captures.
"""

READS = ()

RELATION = frozenset(
    """correlate correlated correlation correlates coincide coincides coinciding
    coincident coincidence conjunction relate related relation relationship relates
    relating linked link links linking tied tie ties tying connected connection connect
    connects associated association associate associates accompanied accompany
    accompanies accompanying combined combine combines combining integrated integrate
    integrating intertwined interrelated interconnected correspond corresponds
    correspondence equivalent equivalence simultaneous simultaneously concurrent
    concurrently mutually alongside coupled couple parallel""".split()
)
LINKING = frozenset("with between to and of in as by from on".split())
RELATION_VALUE = 0.36  # mean activation on relation words
LINKING_VALUE = 0.25  # mean activation on a linking word after one
TYPICAL = -0.02  # the component's mean elsewhere
WINDOW = 3  # tokens after a relation word in which a linking word counts


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    """carry: the position of the most recent relation word in this document, or None."""
    t = prefix.position
    word = prefix.token_strings[-1].strip().lower()
    new_doc = len(prefix.document_ids) > 1 and prefix.document_ids[-1] != prefix.document_ids[-2]
    last = None if (carry is None or new_doc) else carry
    if word in RELATION:
        return t, RELATION_VALUE
    if last is not None and t - last <= WINDOW and word in LINKING:
        return last, LINKING_VALUE
    return last, TYPICAL

"""Layer 15 MLP unit 451 (down_proj component), read as a "weighing alternatives" detector.

What it does: the component's activation sits near its typical level (about -0.1) in plain
text and goes clearly negative while the text doubts itself or weighs options: "Wait, but
maybe ...", "... unless ...", "alternatively ...", "something ... or ...", "constrained by ...",
and question marks in working-out. It turns mildly positive on conclusion words ("so",
"therefore", "thus", "first"). The program scores each token with those rules, and lets the
doubt fade over the following tokens (decay 0.95), so a whole stretch of hesitation counts,
not only the trigger word. A document boundary resets the fade.

Why: when the component is negative, the direction it writes, read through the unembedding,
favours vague next words ("something", "some", "somehow"), so it is part of the model's
hedging. The rules here are a rough summary: a per-token lookup table reaches about 6% of
variance on held-out sample rows, and this program about 5% on eval (correlation 0.22).
Its switch-off effect on the output is small (KL 3.5e-5 nats per position), and the program
reproduces about 81% of it.
"""

READS = ()

# Words that signal doubt, second-guessing or a turn in the reasoning.
DOUBT = {"wait", "hmm", "but", "however", "unless", "alternatively", "actually",
         "maybe", "perhaps", "might", "could", "would", "must", "possibly"}
# Vague, indefinite or conditional words.
VAGUE = {"something", "some", "certain", "another", "such", "possible", "or",
         "depends", "depending", "condition", "conditions", "require", "requires",
         "except", "by", "terms"}
# Words that open a conclusion.
CONCLUDE = {"so", "therefore", "thus", "first", "hence", "yes", "then"}

DECAY = 0.95  # how fast the doubt from earlier tokens fades
FADE = -0.3   # how strongly faded doubt pushes the activation down
BASE = -0.06  # the activation's typical level


def word_of(text):
    """The token's bare lowercase word, without spaces or punctuation."""
    return text.strip().lower().strip("?,.:;()'\"*#`$\\ ")


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    doubt_level, document = carry if carry is not None else (0.0, None)
    if prefix.document_ids[-1] != document:
        doubt_level = 0.0
    document = prefix.document_ids[-1]

    text = prefix.token_strings[-1]
    word = word_of(text)
    now = 0.0
    if word in DOUBT:
        now -= 1.2
    elif word in VAGUE:
        now -= 0.9
    if "?" in text:
        now -= 0.9
    if word in CONCLUDE:
        now += 0.5

    value = BASE + now + FADE * doubt_level
    is_doubt = 1.0 if word in DOUBT else 0.0
    return (DECAY * (doubt_level + is_doubt), document), value

"""Layer 15 MLP down_proj, component 454: a near-silent, diffuse direction.

What the component is: a rank-one piece of the MLP down projection. Its input
direction V is mostly neuron 454 of layer 15's MLP hidden layer (about a fifth of
its squared norm), with the rest spread thinly over thousands of other neurons. Its
activation is the MLP hidden state projected on V, times the norm of its output
direction U.

What this program predicts: no clean concept. Measured on training text, the
activation is 0 at the first token of each document (std 0.004 there) and a small
positive constant (its mean, about 0.02, std 0.26) everywhere else. Held-out token
identity and previous-token lookups explain nothing (about 1% or less), position in
the document explains about 0.1%, and the norms of the residual stream and of the
MLP hidden state have near-zero correlation with it. The only strong correlate is
neuron 454 itself, whose value correlates 0.36 with the activation, and a linear
probe on the residual stream reaches about 0.2 of variance. Neuron 454 has no simple
readable rule either: its largest values occur on code and prose alike, with both
signs. So this program is a baseline: it gets the document-start zero and the mean
right, and nothing more.
"""

READS = ()

MEAN_ACTIVATION = 0.02  # the component's mean away from document starts


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    docs = prefix.document_ids
    first_in_document = len(docs) == 1 or docs[-1] != docs[-2]
    return carry, 0.0 if first_in_document else MEAN_ACTIVATION

"""Component layers.15.mlp.down_proj:455: a "wrap-up word" detector.

In plain terms: this is layer 15's MLP neuron 455 (its down-projection column,
scaled). It is large and positive on words that wrap up or conclude what came
before, and on words that close a list with "and so on":

  * conclusion connectives that open an inference: "Thus", "Therefore", "Hence",
    "Consequently", "So" (as in "So, we ..."), and 因此 / 所以 / 故, なので / だから;
  * list closers: "etc", 等, など;
  * summing-up phrases, at their last word: "Overall", "In short", "As a result",
    "In other words", "That is to say";
  * "total" / "totaling" (weak).

"so" counts only when it opens a clause (after punctuation or "and"); the
intensifier in "so big" / "so easy" is slightly negative, so it is predicted 0.
Everything else is predicted 0, which is close to its typical small noise.

The program is stateless: each position is scored from the newest token and the
text just before it. Its values are the typical activation for each group.
It explains only a small share of the variance (about 5 percent): the
component's variance is mostly in unrelated, context-dependent noise.
"""

import re

READS = ()

# Words that open an inference or a list close: typical activation about 3 to 5.5.
STRONG = {
    "thus", "therefore", "hence", "consequently", "accordingly", "thereby",
    "因此", "所以", "故", "从而", "なので", "だから", "ので",
    "etc", "等", "など",
}
# Summing-up phrases, matched at the end of the text so far: about 1 to 3.
SUMMING_UP = (
    "overall", "in short", "in summary", "in conclusion", "in sum", "to sum up",
    "taken together", "all told", "in total", "altogether", "as a result",
    "in other words", "that is to say", "and so on", "whatever", "otherwise",
)
# What comes before a word that starts a new clause.
CLAUSE_STARTS = {".", ",", ";", ":", "!", "?", "\n", "。", "，", ")", ""}


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    t = prefix.position
    word = prefix.token_strings[t].strip().lower()
    same_doc = t > 0 and prefix.document_ids[t - 1] == prefix.document_ids[t]
    before = prefix.token_strings[t - 1].strip() if same_doc else ""
    tail = re.sub(r"\s+", " ", prefix.text_prefixes[t][-30:].lower()) if same_doc else ""

    if word in STRONG:
        value = 4.0
    elif tail.endswith(SUMMING_UP):
        value = 2.0
    elif word == "so":
        value = 3.0 if before in CLAUSE_STARTS or before in {"and", "but"} else 0.0
    elif word in {"total", "totaling", "totals"}:
        value = 1.0
    else:
        value = 0.0
    return carry, value

"""Decimal-point detector: the component fires on the '.' (or a digit-group
',' or time ':') that comes right after a number.

Its output is written into the residual stream at each position. The model
reads it at the separator, where the next token may be the fractional digits
of a number, so the component is largest on a decimal point after a number
of one to three digits ("3.", "49.", "0.") and weaker after a long number,
after a list label at the start of a line ("3. Blooms") or after a comma or
colon in a number ("9,000", "12:30").

step() looks back over the digit tokens just before the current token, in the
same document, to count the number's digits and to check whether it begins a
line. It returns one value per position: the component's predicted activation.
"""

READS = ()

# Typical activation after each separator, by what precedes it.
DOT_AFTER_NUMBER = 2.3      # '.' after 1-3 digits: "3.14", "$49.99"
DOT_AFTER_LONG = 0.9        # '.' after 4 or more digits: "2009.", "15000."
DOT_LIST_LABEL = 0.6        # '.' after a line-initial number: "1. First"
SEP_AFTER_NUMBER = {",": 0.2, ":": 0.4}  # ',' or ':' after digits: "9,000", "12:30"


def _is_digit(s):
    return s.strip().isdigit() and s.strip().isascii()


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    toks = prefix.token_strings
    docs = prefix.document_ids
    cur = toks[-1].strip()
    if cur not in (".", ",", ":"):
        return carry, 0.0

    # Count the digit tokens directly before the separator, in the same document.
    run, j = 0, len(toks) - 2
    while j >= 0 and docs[j] == docs[-1] and _is_digit(toks[j]):
        run += 1
        j -= 1
    if run == 0:
        return carry, 0.0

    if cur in SEP_AFTER_NUMBER:
        return carry, SEP_AFTER_NUMBER[cur]

    # Is the number at the start of a line? Skip spaces back to a newline.
    k = j
    while k >= 0 and docs[k] == docs[-1] and toks[k].strip() == "" and "\n" not in toks[k]:
        k -= 1
    line_start = k < 0 or docs[k] != docs[-1] or "\n" in toks[k]
    if line_start:
        return carry, DOT_LIST_LABEL
    return carry, DOT_AFTER_LONG if run >= 4 else DOT_AFTER_NUMBER

"""Layer 15, MLP hidden unit 459 (this component), read as a few plain rules.

The unit is a gate: it opens hard in citation-like text (journal and case-reporter
references, abbreviations such as "Phys.", "Amer.", "F.3d"), and its sign then depends
on the token. Two of its clearest effects are written here:

- the period that closes a short capitalised abbreviation goes positive
  ("Phys.", "Amer.", "F." in "702 F.3d");
- a digit inside a decimal fraction, from its second digit on ("0.8[4]"),
  goes negative.

Everything else predicts 0. Measured on eval rows, these two rules explain under 1%
of the variance (r about 0.1): the rest is a sparse signal whose sign depends on
context this program does not model. Switching the component off changes the model
very little (KL about 8e-6 nats per position), so the rules matter little end to end.
"""

import re

READS = ()

ABBREVIATION = re.compile(r" ?[A-Z][A-Za-z]{0,4}")
DIGIT = re.compile(r"[0-9]")
PERIOD_AFTER_ABBREVIATION = 0.9
DECIMAL_DIGIT_AFTER_FIRST = -1.0


def is_digit(text):
    return DIGIT.fullmatch(text) is not None


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    tokens = prefix.token_strings
    docs = prefix.document_ids
    n = len(tokens)
    cur = tokens[n - 1]
    value = 0.0
    if n >= 2 and docs[n - 1] == docs[n - 2]:
        if cur == ".":
            if ABBREVIATION.fullmatch(tokens[n - 2]):
                value = PERIOD_AFTER_ABBREVIATION
        elif is_digit(cur) and is_digit(tokens[n - 2]):
            # walk back over the digit run; a decimal fraction has a '.' before it
            k = n - 2
            while k >= 0 and docs[k] == docs[n - 1] and is_digit(tokens[k]):
                k -= 1
            # tokens[k] is the token before the run; the run starts at k + 1
            if k >= 1 and tokens[k] == "." and is_digit(tokens[k - 1]):
                value = DECIMAL_DIGIT_AFTER_FIRST
    return carry, value

"""Agent-"by" detector.

Component p-82af68dd@100000/layers.15.mlp.down_proj:461 writes a strong negative value
whenever the current token is the preposition "by" introducing the doer or the means of
an action ("written by", "caused by", "by using ..."). The same preposition in other
languages ("par", "por", "pela", "oleh", "durch") gives a smaller negative value.
Mathematical or ordering uses ("divided by", "multiplied by", "step by step") are nearly
silent. Every other token gets 0: the component's remaining variation is small,
diffuse and not explained by word identity.
"""

AGENT_BY = -4.5  # "by" after a verb or noun: the doer or means of an action
MATH_BY = -1.0  # "by" in "divided by", "multiplied by", "step by step"
FOREIGN_BY = {"par", "por", "pela", "pelo", "oleh", "durch"}  # the same preposition
FOREIGN_VALUE = -2.0
MATH_BEFORE = {"divided", "divide", "multiplied", "multiply", "times", "step", "steps"}

READS = ()


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    word = prefix.token_strings[-1].strip().lower()
    if word == "by":
        same_doc = len(prefix.document_ids) > 1 and prefix.document_ids[-2] == prefix.document_ids[-1]
        before = prefix.token_strings[-2].strip().lower() if same_doc else ""
        return carry, MATH_BY if before in MATH_BEFORE else AGENT_BY
    if word in FOREIGN_BY:
        return carry, FOREIGN_VALUE
    return carry, 0.0

"""Layer 15 MLP hidden unit 462, as the component p-82af68dd@100000/layers.15.mlp.down_proj:462.

What the component is: its activation is (MLP hidden vector . V) * ||U||, and V is almost
entirely hidden unit 462 of layer 15's MLP (weight 0.97), so the component is that unit's
output, scaled. Its size is largest on the later pieces of a word that the tokenizer split into
several tokens (a "mid-word" piece), most of all for Greek and Cyrillic words, and smallest on
Chinese, Japanese and Korean characters. Its sign is not set by anything simple in the text:
the same kind of token goes both ways, and the tokens' identities explain almost none of it.

What this program does: it predicts the average activation for each class of token, where the
class is the token's script plus whether it continues a word begun by the token before it. The
averages come from 8,192 training rows. They are small, so the program predicts values near
zero and captures only the class-level offsets. It does not predict the large swings.
"""

import regex

READS = ()

# Mean activation per (script, continues a word) class, from training text.
MEAN = {
    ("greek", True): 0.163,
    ("greek", False): 0.062,
    ("cyrillic", True): 0.007,
    ("cyrillic", False): -0.058,
    ("cjk", True): -0.070,
    ("cjk", False): -0.014,
    ("latin", True): -0.035,
    ("latin", False): -0.061,
    ("other", True): -0.034,
    ("other", False): 0.001,
    ("digit", False): 0.028,
    ("punct", False): 0.015,
    ("space", False): 0.020,
}

SCRIPTS = (
    ("greek", r"\p{Greek}"),
    ("cyrillic", r"\p{Cyrillic}"),
    ("cjk", r"\p{Han}|\p{Hiragana}|\p{Katakana}|\p{Hangul}"),
    ("latin", r"\p{Latin}"),
)


def script_of(token):
    """The token's script class, read from its first visible character."""
    text = token.strip()
    if not text:
        return "space"
    for name, pattern in SCRIPTS:
        if regex.match(pattern, text[0]):
            return name
    if text[0].isalpha():
        return "other"
    return "digit" if text[0].isdigit() else "punct"


def is_letters(token):
    """Whether a token is a run of letters, such as part of a word."""
    return token.strip().isalpha()


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    """Predict the component's activation at the newest token."""
    cur = prefix.token_strings[-1]
    continues = False
    if prefix.position > 0 and prefix.document_ids[-2] == prefix.document_ids[-1]:
        # A word piece: letters right after letters, with no space before it.
        prev = prefix.token_strings[-2]
        continues = is_letters(prev) and is_letters(cur) and not cur[:1].isspace()
    return carry, MEAN.get((script_of(cur), continues), 0.0)

"""Word-level guess at layers.15.mlp.down_proj:463 (a rank-one piece of the layer-15 MLP output).

What the data shows: the component is positive on words that leave a slot unspecified or
generic ("something", "certain", "some", "specific", "appropriate", "amount", "threshold"),
and negative on words that pick out particular items or count and order them ("two", "first",
"other", "another", "both", "this", "these", "each"). Almost every other token sits at a
small negative baseline. Its activation at the first token of a document is about zero.

What this program does: it looks only at the current word, puts it in one of those three
groups, and returns the group's typical value. It explains only a little of the activation:
most of the variance depends on context (the component's activation is correlated from token
to token, and what the model expects next), which a word list cannot capture.
"""

READS = ()

UNSPECIFIED = {
    "something", "someone", "somebody", "somewhere", "somehow", "whatever", "anything",
    "certain", "some", "specific", "specified", "appropriate", "respective", "particular",
    "threshold", "amount", "quantity", "percentage", "fraction", "variable", "suitable",
    "relevant", "desired", "unknown", "name",
}
ENUMERATIVE = {
    "two", "three", "four", "five", "first", "second", "other", "another", "one", "both",
    "this", "these", "those", "each",
}

BASELINE = -0.02
UNSPECIFIED_VALUE = 0.43
ENUMERATIVE_VALUE = -0.2


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    if prefix.position == 0:
        return carry, 0.0
    word = prefix.token_strings[-1].strip().lower()
    if word in UNSPECIFIED:
        return carry, UNSPECIFIED_VALUE
    if word in ENUMERATIVE:
        return carry, ENUMERATIVE_VALUE
    return carry, BASELINE

"""Layer 15 MLP down_proj, component 464: a weak detector for punctuation inside code brackets.

What it responds to, in plain terms:
- Strongest: the commas and the closing ')' of a function's parameter list,
  e.g. `func f(a T, b U) error`, `def f(self, x):`, `int main(int argc, ...)`.
- Strong: commas, semicolons and line breaks or indentation inside any other open
  bracket: call arguments, lists, dicts, for-loop headers, code blocks.
- Weak: the same tokens at top level, outside any bracket, in prose or text.
- Near zero or slightly negative: identifiers, numbers and punctuation like ':' and '.'.

It reads only the text so far: the stack of open brackets in the current document
(brackets reset at a new document), and the current token. The values are the mean
activation of each group on sample training text, so the program predicts the group
average. The activation is not a clean function of any of these, so most of its
variance stays unexplained.
"""

import re
from collections.abc import Mapping

READS: tuple[str, ...] = ()

# A '(' opened on a line with one of these words starts a function's parameter list.
DEF_WORDS = (
    r"func|def|function|fn|void|async|public|private|protected|static"
    r"|int|char|float|double|bool|string|String"
)
DEF_WORD = re.compile(r"\b(" + DEF_WORDS + r")\b")

# Mean activation of each group, measured on sample training text.
SIG_COMMA = 3.0  # ',' inside a parameter list
SIG_CLOSE = 1.8  # ')' closing a parameter list
SIG_OTHER = 0.1  # any other token inside a parameter list
IN_COMMA = 0.75  # ',' inside another bracket
IN_SEMI = 0.28  # ';' or '{' or '}' inside a bracket
IN_SPACE = 0.46  # newline or indentation inside a bracket
OUT_COMMA = 0.1  # ',' at top level
OUT_SEMI = 0.27  # ';' '{' '}' at top level
OUT_SPACE = 0.1  # newline or indentation at top level
WORD = -0.11  # identifiers, numbers, and other text
PUNCT = -0.09  # ':' and '.' and other punctuation
OPEN = -0.09  # opening brackets


def step(carry, prefix, upstream: Mapping):
    doc = prefix.document_ids[-1]
    if carry is None or carry["doc"] != doc:
        carry = {"doc": doc, "stack": [], "line": ""}
    stack, line = carry["stack"], carry["line"]
    token = prefix.token_strings[-1]

    # Brackets open before this token decide where it sits.
    inside = bool(stack)
    in_sig = inside and stack[-1] == "sig"
    closes_sig = False
    for ch in token:
        if ch == "\n":
            line = ""
            continue
        if ch == "(":
            stack.append("sig" if DEF_WORD.search(line) else "(")
        elif ch in "[{":
            stack.append(ch)
        elif ch in ")]}":
            if stack and stack.pop() == "sig":
                closes_sig = True
        line += ch
    carry = {"doc": doc, "stack": stack[-64:], "line": line[-200:]}

    has_comma = "," in token
    has_semi = any(ch in token for ch in ";{}")
    if in_sig and has_comma:
        return carry, SIG_COMMA
    if closes_sig:
        return carry, SIG_CLOSE
    if in_sig:
        return carry, SIG_OTHER
    if token.strip() == "":
        return carry, (IN_SPACE if inside else OUT_SPACE)
    if has_comma:
        return carry, IN_COMMA if inside else OUT_COMMA
    if has_semi:
        return carry, IN_SEMI if inside else OUT_SEMI
    if re.fullmatch(r"\s*\w+\s*", token):
        return carry, WORD

What it does: the component is a "a subject has just been written, and a verb is due"
signal. Its activation is large and positive on subject pronouns (I, he, she, we, they, and
it / you more weakly), most of all when the pronoun opens a new clause (right after
punctuation or a conjunction). It is also positive on "who" (a relative pronoun that is a
subject) and mildly on articles and prepositions (a, an, in, to, is). It is negative on
clause-linking words (but, so, that, which, when, because, also, now, only) and on modal
and auxiliary verbs (can, could, must, have, does), which come before a verb rather than a
subject. Everything else is about zero.

This is a hand-written rule with a few word classes and weights, fit by least squares to the
component's activations on 2M training tokens. It looks only at the current token and the one
before it.
"""

from collections.abc import Mapping

READS: tuple[str, ...] = ()

# Subject pronouns, and their equivalents in a few other languages.
STRONG_SUBJECT = {"i", "he", "she", "we", "they", "我", "他", "她", "我们", "他们",
                  "я", "он", "она", "мы", "они", "ich", "er", "sie", "wir", "il", "elle",
                  "nous", "ils"}
WEAK_SUBJECT = {"it", "you", "它", "你", "ты", "du", "es", "vous", "tu"}
RELATIVE_SUBJECT = {"who"}

# Clause linkers and adverbs, which pull the activation down.
CONNECTIVES = {"but", "so", "that", "which", "when", "where", "while", "because", "as",
               "also", "now", "just", "only", "how", "why", "then", "than", "however",
               "moreover", "although", "though", "thus", "yet", "whenever", "once",
               "currently", "whether", "perhaps", "these", "very", "most", "if"}

# Modal and auxiliary verbs, which come before a verb.
AUXILIARIES = {"can", "could", "should", "must", "might", "may", "have", "had", "has", "do",
               "did", "does", "would", "be", "been", "being", "shall", "am", "are", "were"}

# Articles and prepositions, which are mildly positive.
ARTICLES_PREPOSITIONS = {"a", "an", "in", "to", "on", "there", "here", "this", "one", "is",
                         "will", "was", "at", "for", "into", "over", "or"}

# Tokens after which a new clause begins: punctuation or a conjunction.
CLAUSE_OPENERS = {".", "!", "?", ",", ";", ":", '"', "“", "(", "and", "but", "so", "when",
                  "if", "that", "because", "as", "while", "where", "though", "although",
                  "then", "until", "since", "unless", "or", "after", "before", "which",
                  "who", "how", "what", "why", "now", "however", "once", ""}

PRONOUN_WEIGHT = 1.14          # subject pronoun inside a clause
WEAK_PRONOUN_WEIGHT = 0.73     # "it" / "you" inside a clause
CLAUSE_START_BONUS = 1.37      # extra for a strong pronoun that opens its clause
WEAK_CLAUSE_BONUS = 0.84       # extra for "it" / "you" that open a clause
RELATIVE_WEIGHT = 0.48
CONNECTIVE_WEIGHT = -0.34
AUXILIARY_WEIGHT = -0.11
ARTICLE_WEIGHT = 0.13


def step(carry, prefix, upstream: Mapping):
    """Activation at this position, from the current token and the token before it."""
    word = prefix.token_strings[-1].strip().lower()
    opens_clause = len(prefix.token_ids) == 1 or prefix.document_ids[-2] != prefix.document_ids[-1]
    if not opens_clause:
        opens_clause = prefix.token_strings[-2].strip().lower() in CLAUSE_OPENERS
    if word in STRONG_SUBJECT:
        value = PRONOUN_WEIGHT + (CLAUSE_START_BONUS if opens_clause else 0.0)
    elif word in WEAK_SUBJECT:
        value = WEAK_PRONOUN_WEIGHT + (WEAK_CLAUSE_BONUS if opens_clause else 0.0)
    elif word in RELATIVE_SUBJECT:
        value = RELATIVE_WEIGHT
    elif word in CONNECTIVES:
        value = CONNECTIVE_WEIGHT
    elif word in AUXILIARIES:
        value = AUXILIARY_WEIGHT
    elif word in ARTICLES_PREPOSITIONS:
        value = ARTICLE_WEIGHT
    else:
        value = 0.0

Layer 15's MLP has a component whose activation is strongly negative on the colon

comment markers ("//", "#"), JSON-style key colons ('":'), and "):".
Everywhere else it is near zero.

Within a document the colon's strength fades as colons pile up: the first colon is
about -4, the tenth about -2. So the program counts the colons seen so far in the
current document (the carry resets when the document changes) and divides by
1 + 0.1 * count. A colon that ends a code header ("try:", "else:") is weaker in the
data; this does not model that.

# Comment markers and key/value openers.
OPENERS = {"//", " //", "#", " #", "///", " ///", "###", '":', "):", "->"}

What it does: this component writes a small signal into the residual stream whose
size (about 0.3 RMS) is not set by any token identity. The program predicts only the
coarse tendency that was measured on training text:

  * the first token of every document (and of every packed row) gives 0;
  * otherwise the value depends on the kind of the current token:
    whitespace and punctuation lean slightly positive, plain words slightly negative,
    CJK characters more negative, digits and everything else near zero.

Why so little: the activation is not a function of the current token (per-token means
do not generalise to held-out text), nor of the previous token, nor of recent-context
averages of token kinds. Most of its variance is within documents, not between them.
Its contribution to the model's output is negligible (switching it off changes
next-token loss by about 1e-5 nats). So this program is a coarse description, not a
mechanism; on eval it explains about 0.2% of the variance (Pearson r about 0.04), and
its effect on the model is about the same as switching the component off.

import re
from collections.abc import Mapping

READS: tuple[str, ...] = ()

# Mean activation by kind of token, measured on 2048 training rows (document starts excluded).
MEAN_BY_KIND = {
    "space": 0.018,
    "punct": 0.013,
    "digit": 0.002,
    "word": -0.017,
    "cjk": -0.025,
    "other": -0.006,
}


def kind(text: str) -> str:
    """Coarse character class of one decoded token."""
    s = text.strip()
    if s == "":
        return "space"
    if re.fullmatch(r"\d+", s):
        return "digit"
    if re.search(r"[぀-ヿ一-鿿]", s):
        return "cjk"
    if re.fullmatch(r"[^\w\s]+", s):
        return "punct"
    if re.fullmatch(r"[A-Za-z]+", s):
        return "word"
    return "other"


def step(carry, prefix, upstream: Mapping):
    # The first token of a row or of a document gives (almost exactly) 0.
    if prefix.position == 0 or prefix.document_ids[-1] != prefix.document_ids[-2]:
        return carry, 0.0
    return carry, MEAN_BY_KIND[kind(prefix.token_strings[-1])]

"""Layer 15 MLP down_proj, component 470: a "code control-flow keyword" detector.

What it does, in plain terms: this component fires most on the keywords that open a
statement in source code: `if`, `return`, `assert`, `while`, `print`, `len`, and the
`(!` of `if (!x)`. It fires more weakly on comparison and call tokens (`==`, `=`, `(`,
`in`, `not`) and on a bare `for`, and it is larger when the surrounding text is code
(brackets, semicolons, dots and underscores in the last few tokens) than when it is prose.
Everything else is predicted as roughly zero, with a slight negative on the words
"The", "this" and "with", which it leans slightly against.

This explains only a few percent of the variance: most of the component's activation is
a dense, context-dependent signal that no token list captures.
"""
import re

READS = ()

WINDOW = 24  # tokens of recent context used to judge whether the text is code
CODE_CHAR = re.compile(r"[{};()=<>\[\]_]|\.(?=[a-zA-Z])|\n\s")
STATEMENT_KEYWORDS = {"if", "return", "assert", "while", "print", "len", "elif", "log", "println", "expect", "await", "isinstance"}
EXPRESSION_TOKENS = {"(!", "!(", "==", "=", "(", "in", "not"}
PROSE_WORDS = {"The", "this", "with"}


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    # carry: (document id, recent code-ness flags of the last WINDOW tokens in this document)
    doc = prefix.document_ids[-1]
    if carry is None or carry[0] != doc:
        flags = []
    else:
        flags = carry[1]
    token = prefix.token_strings[-1]
    word = token.strip()

    # how code-like the recent text is: share of recent tokens with code characters
    density = sum(flags) / len(flags) if flags else 0.0

    if word in STATEMENT_KEYWORDS:
        value = 2.0 * (0.3 + 2.0 * density)
    elif word == "for":
        value = 0.8 * density
    elif word in EXPRESSION_TOKENS:
        value = 0.6 * density
    elif word in PROSE_WORDS:
        value = -0.1
    else:
        value = 0.0

    # the current token joins the context for the next position
    flags = (flags + [1 if CODE_CHAR.search(token) else 0])[-WINDOW:]
    return (doc, flags), float(value)

names (`/workspace/app/src/core/options.ts`, `tests/unit/x.py`, `./utils/aria`) and on
import lines, and is near zero in ordinary prose. The program reads the text so far and
tracks the word and the line the current token is in (both reset at a new document).

  -5  a path word naming a project folder or test (test, src, workspace, bed, lib, ...),
      containing a slash, dot or underscore, e.g. `/src`, `.test`, `_test`, `testbed`
  -4  a word ending in a source-code file extension (.py, .ts, .go, .rs, ...)
  -2  any other path word: a slash between letters, or a leading `/`, `./` or `../`
  -2  a token on a line that starts with import / from / include / require / use
  -2  a URL (http://, https://, www.)
  0   everything else
"""

READS = ()

PROJECT = re.compile(r"test|src|workspace|bed|lib|bin|spec|pkg|node_modules|main")
CODE_EXT = re.compile(r"\.(py|go|ts|tsx|js|jsx|rs|java|php|rb|c|h|cc|cpp|cs|vue|kt|swift|scala)$")
PATH = re.compile(r"[A-Za-z0-9_.-]/[A-Za-z0-9_.-]|^\.{0,2}/")
IMPORT_LINE = re.compile(r"^\s*(import|from|#include|require|use|using|package)\b")
DELIMS = "\"'(),;<>[]{}=`|"

    for ch in prefix.token_strings[-1]:
        if ch in "\r\n":

        elif ch.isspace() or ch in DELIMS:
            word, line = "", (line + ch)[-60:]

        value = -5.0
    elif CODE_EXT.search(word):
        value = -4.0
    elif PATH.search(word):
        value = -2.0
    elif IMPORT_LINE.match(line):

    else:

    return (word, line, doc), value

"""Rough predictor for layers.15.mlp.down_proj component 503.

What it responds to, in plain terms (fit on ~1k rows of the training data):
  * Token kind of the current token:
      - file-extension tokens (".py", ".js", ".go", ".php", ".yml", ...)  -> up
      - units and superscripts ("°", "°C", "²", "³", "℃")               -> strongly up
      - whitespace-only and punctuation tokens                         -> down
  * Capitalised names: a capitalised word that follows another capitalised
    word (the 2nd+ word of a name like "Hyundai Heavy Industries")        -> up
  * Repetition: the text just read has occurred earlier in the same
    document (the current token ends a run of 2+ tokens already seen
    there). Longer repeats raise the prediction more than short ones.
  * Position 0 of a row (no context) is ~0.

It explains only a few percent of the variance; the component is diffuse.
"""

import re

EXT = re.compile(r"\.[A-Za-z0-9]{1,6}")
UNIT = re.compile(r"[²³°℃]+|°C|/m[Ll]|/hr")
CAP = re.compile(r"[A-Z][a-z].*|[A-Z]{2,}.*")
PUNCT = re.compile(r"[^\w\s]+")
MAX_MATCH = 32  # longest repeat length we measure
RECENT = 50  # earlier occurrences of a token we check per position

READS = ()


def _kind(s):
    """Token kind from its text: returns (is_file_ext, is_unit, is_capitalised, is_space, is_punct)."""
    c = s.strip()
    return (
        bool(EXT.fullmatch(c)),
        bool(UNIT.fullmatch(c)),
        bool(CAP.fullmatch(c)),
        c == "",
        bool(PUNCT.fullmatch(c)),
    )


def _match_len(ids, s, i):
    """How many tokens back from i agree with the tokens back from s (s < i)."""
    k = 0
    while k < MAX_MATCH and s - k >= 0 and ids[s - k] == ids[i - k]:
        k += 1
    return k


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    t = prefix.position
    tok = prefix.token_ids[-1]
    doc = prefix.document_ids[-1]
    if carry is None or carry["doc"] != doc:
        carry = {"doc": doc, "ids": [], "where": {}, "kinds": []}
    ids, where = carry["ids"], carry["where"]
    ids.append(tok)
    i = len(ids) - 1
    # longest earlier repeat of the text ending here, within this document
    run = 0
    for s in where.get(tok, [])[-RECENT:]:
        run = max(run, _match_len(ids, s, i))
    where.setdefault(tok, []).append(i)
    is_ext, is_unit, is_cap, is_space, is_punct = _kind(prefix.token_strings[-1])
    carry["kinds"].append(is_cap)
    if t == 0:
        return carry, 0.0
    value = 0.2
    value += 0.8 * is_ext + 2.0 * is_unit
    value += 0.1 * is_cap - 0.5 * is_space - 0.2 * is_punct
    # a capitalised word right after another capitalised word in the same document
    if is_cap and len(carry["kinds"]) >= 2 and carry["kinds"][-2]:
        value += 0.8
    # repeated text earlier in the document
    if run >= 4:
        value += 0.7 if run <= 10 else 0.5
    elif run >= 2:
        value += 0.5
    return carry, value

What it does, in plain terms: a small, diffuse feature. It is positive on the words a
mathematical argument uses to state a necessary consequence ("must", "so", "therefore",
"implies", "either", "only", "equal", "true", "constant", and the arrows → and ⇒), and
strongly positive inside such deductions, e.g. "Therefore, h(x) - x^2 must be a constant".
It is negative on programming syntax ("return", "->", "public", indented code) and mildly
negative on the equals sign. Almost everywhere else it sits near zero.

This program only looks at the current token: it predicts a fixed value per word class,
with no memory of earlier tokens. It explains very little of the variance (about 0.4% on
sampled training text), because the component's large swings depend on context that a
word list cannot see.
"""

# Words that state a necessity or a consequence, as in a proof.
DEDUCTION = {
    "must", "either", "only", "equal", "implies", "therefore", "so", "then",
    "true", "constant", "unless", "hence", "thus", "consequently",
}
ARROWS = {"→", "⇒"}

# Programming keywords and rewrite arrows, where the component goes negative.
CODE = {"return", "public", "private", "void", "static", "->"}

SCALE = 0.3


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    word = prefix.token_strings[-1].strip()
    if word.lower() in DEDUCTION or word in ARROWS:

about 0.29. It is not explained by the current token (R^2 ~ 0.001), the previous token

"""Sentence-end detector for layers.15 mlp.down_proj component 507.

This component writes a large positive value into the residual stream when the
current token closes a full sentence of ordinary prose: a period after a word,
a question mark, exclamation mark, or Chinese/fullwidth full stop, or a period
closing a bracket or quote (").", ”.", %.). It is near zero on most other tokens.
A period after a number or after a capitalised word (Dr., Fig., Vol.) is weak,
since those periods usually do not end a sentence.

Predicted activation per token (the component's activation, roughly):
  ? ! ！ ？ 。                -> STRONG  (about 3.5)
  ). ]. ". ”. %. etc.        -> CLOSER  (about 3.5)
  "." after a lowercase word -> PROSE   (about 4.5)
  "." after a digit or a capitalised word -> WEAK (about 1)
  anything else              -> 0
Tokens are matched exactly, so ".\n" (a period at a line end) is not a sentence end.
"""

READS = ()

STRONG = 3.5
CLOSER = 3.5
PROSE = 4.5
WEAK = 1.0

CLOSING = ')]}"\'”’`%$'


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    tok = prefix.token_strings[-1]
    prev = prefix.token_strings[-2].strip() if prefix.position > 0 else ""
    if tok in ("?", "!", "！", "？", "。"):
        return carry, STRONG
    if tok == ".":
        if prev[-1:].isdigit() or prev[:1].isupper():
            return carry, WEAK
        if prev.isalpha() and prev.islower():
            return carry, PROSE
        return carry, 0.0
    if len(tok) > 1 and tok[-1] == "." and tok[-2] in CLOSING:
        return carry, CLOSER
    return carry, 0.0

Its activation is a small, signed, diffuse value (mean about -0.07, std about 0.37). Most of
its variance is not explained by any token, bigram or simple context rule I tried. The
largest values are on a few word types, and this program predicts them:

- Positive on "to" and connectives that open a purpose, reason or avoidance clause:

  "worried about". The component's output direction promotes "avoid"-type continuations.
- Negative on "to" after a verb or adjective that takes an infinitive complement ("tried to",
  "forced to", "decided to", "likely to", "best to"), where the next word is an ordinary

- Elsewhere it predicts the mean.

MEAN = -0.07  # typical activation at ordinary tokens

RULES = {
    (None, " because"): 0.7,
    (None, " without"): 0.7,
    (" due", " to"): 0.8,
    (" Due", " to"): 0.8,
    (" to", " avoid"): 1.4,
    (" to", " prevent"): 0.7,
    (" because", " of"): 0.6,
    (" instead", " of"): 0.4,
    (" result", " of"): -0.45,
    (" worried", " about"): 2.0,
    (" concern", " about"): 2.0,
}

# complement, not a purpose, and the component is negative there
INFINITIVE_HOSTS = {
    " tried", " tries", " try", " forced", " asked", " decided", " refused", " agreed",
    " wanted", " wants", " likely", " expected", " seem", " seems", " appear", " appears",
    " tend", " tends", " supposed", " sure", " best", " committed", " known", " going",
    " like", " began", " set", " led", " choose", " attempts",
}


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    toks = prefix.token_strings
    cur = toks[-1]

    if len(toks) > 1 and prefix.document_ids[-2] == prefix.document_ids[-1]:
